column1: # PB-APP-9 traceability: every error class the facade exports -> the state the user is
# shown and what they can do about it. Enforced in THREE directions, none of which trusts
#   - mobile/s16_taxonomy_test.go   class_const and token are set-compared against
#                                   is read from the CONSTANT's source rather than from
#                                   here -- so a drifted row fails instead of misrouting;
#   - android/gate/s16_ui_test.go   rendered_state is set-compared against the Kotlin
#                                   `enum class ErrorState`, and every token must appear
#   - mobile/conformance/s16_errorstates_test.go  every row is reachable: an adversarial
#                                   state matrix sweeps the whole golden surface and no
#                                   error may land outside this table.
# Columns: class_const <TAB> token <TAB> sentinel <TAB> rendered_state <TAB> remedy <TAB> requirement <TAB> note
# `sentinel` is the Go error IDENTITY the class classifies, or "-" for a class the facade
# authors itself. `rendered_state` is a constant of dev.swarm.phone.ui.ErrorState.
# `remedy` is what the user (or the machine) must do; the three of PB-APP-10 are
# authenticate / re_pair / machine_regrant and they may never collapse.

column7: RESERVED. App.ErrorClass answers this for a message the facade did not produce, and for nothing else. It is what makes the exhaustiveness sweep a real assertion: a classifier that could not say "I do not know this" would satisfy every other check by answering one class for everything.
A panic caught at the JNI boundary, or a foreign error identity nothing routes. Never the user's fault and never has a user action, which is why it must not share a state with anything that does.

A screen passed something the facade cannot use: an empty session id, a nil spec, a stream name that is not one of the four repair channels. Same remedy as INTERNAL and a different state, because the app is otherwise healthy and one call was wrong.

A lookup that legitimately misses -- a session no longer in the roster, a snapshot never received, an index past the end of a handle. Distinct from INVALID_REQUEST: nothing is wrong with the call, the thing is simply gone.
A call on an App the Android lifecycle already closed. Its own class because it is the one failure a screen fixes by doing nothing: the next launch constructs a new App.
The transport: not started, no connection yet, or the relay refused or dropped the call. The ONE class for which a spinner is honest -- every other waiting state here has something the user must do.

The phone holds no machine destination. NOT the same as REPAIR_REQUIRED: nothing is broken and no owner has revoked anything -- this handset has simply never completed a pairing that pinned a destination.

PB-STATE-4's fail-closed refusal of a durable blob that will not load. It was ErrClassInternal until S18b, i.e. remedy report_bug over a state the owner CAN recover from -- the brick expressed as a screen. Its remedy is its own because it is TWO acts and neither alone works: the user clears the app's data, and the OWNER unregisters the device at the machine, or the re-pair the advice ends in is refused (PB-KEY-3). It does not offer the pairing flow: there is no App to offer it from, the blob having failed Resume.

PB-KEY-8's two refusals -- a capability the handset does not provide, and a key read back WEAKER than requested. Raised on the Android side (KeyCustodyException.PlatformCapabilityMissing / KeystoreDowngrade, routed by PhoneRuntime), so the sentinel column is "-": the Go facade has no identity for a Keystore read-back. Same remedy as INTERNAL and a different state, for INVALID_REQUEST's reason inverted: the APP is healthy and the platform is not, so a message blaming the app is false. It must never be re_pair -- a re-pair re-provisions the same key on the same handset and returns to this screen, which is PB-APP-10's forbidden loop reached through the remedy.
PB-SYNC-7's fail-closed refusal of mutating ops until the machine publishes its rollback authorities. Reads keep working throughout, so the screen shows a banner and not an error page.

No epoch content key, and the grant has NOT been proved lost. This is the ordinary first-launch window; rendering it as GRANT_LOST would send a healthy user to the machine for a key that is already on its way.

The one remedy the USER cannot perform. It may never collapse into REPAIR_REQUIRED: BeginPairing fail-fasts while this device is registered (PB-STATE-10), so "pair again" is advice that cannot be carried out and the only exit left is physical access to the machine.

RECOVERABLE. Prompt for the biometric; the operation is worth retrying afterwards. The token is the one Kotlin has matched on since S14 (GoCustodyFailure.AUTH_REQUIRED_TOKEN); it is deliberately not re-spelled.
PERMANENT. The Keystore key is destroyed and no prompt brings it back. Same token discipline as the row above; a drifted copy degrades this into a prompt the user can never satisfy.

The OWNER removed this device. It shares REPAIR_REQUIRED's remedy and not its cause, which is why it is a class of its own: the machine still holds a registration the owner must clear before a re-pair can succeed. Without this row a revoked phone redials every 250 ms behind a spinner forever.
The machine has not confirmed a control lease, so every keystroke -- and PB-APP-3's Stop -- is refused. The screen's remedy is to offer take-control; a retry is the one thing that cannot help.
A bound this phone enforces on itself (the section 6.0 resync budget) or the relay enforces on it. Retryable only after waiting: "asking harder" is exactly what the bound exists to stop.

The class for errors the pairing VERBS return. The pairing attempt's own terminal state is on the Pairing handle and is finer grained (PB-PAIR-5's five values); this is what a screen shows when the call itself failed.
